# Epic Games Lawsuit: Every Fortnite Case and Who Actually Gets Paid

**Active Litigation**

Claim deadline wasJuly 9, 2025 · as of Oct 13, 2026

[Get a free case review](#review)[Can I still file?](#can-i-file)

As of September 30, 2026, the only Epic Games settlement paying U.S. players that we track is the FTC’s Fortnite refund — and its claims closed on July 9, 2025. A third payment round is still promised for 2026, with no date. The “Epic Games class action” in the September 2026 headlines is a claim by a Dutch foundation on behalf of Dutch players. Epic’s fights with Apple and Google are business cases with no consumer payout, and the Apple case is now before the U.S. Supreme Court.

We are not a claims administrator and not affiliated with any settlement. File only at the official settlement website — filing is always free.

## Five Different Fights Under One Name

“Epic Games lawsuit” covers cases that have almost nothing in common except Fortnite.  
  
**1. The FTC case (2022).** According to the FTC, Epic used design tricks known as **dark patterns** to charge players for purchases they did not want, let children run up charges without a parent’s permission, and locked some accounts after players disputed charges. Separately, the FTC alleged that Epic collected personal information from children under 13 without parental consent. Epic agreed to pay **$520 million**: a **$245 million** refund order and a **$275 million** COPPA penalty. Only the $245 million pays players.  
  
**2. Epic v. Apple.** Apple and Google both removed Fortnite from their app stores on August 13, 2020, after Epic changed how players could buy V-Bucks, and Epic sued. Epic largely lost against Apple, but a 2021 ruling barred Apple from stopping developers from pointing users to other ways to pay. In April 2025 the trial judge found Apple had violated that order.  
  
**3. Epic v. Google.** A jury sided with Epic in December 2023, finding Google’s Play Store practices anticompetitive.  
  
**4. Player class actions.** In March 2025, two parents filed a proposed U.S. class action alleging that Fortnite’s Item Shop countdown timers were deceptive. In September 2026 a Dutch foundation began a mass claim on behalf of young Dutch players.  
  
**5. Addiction lawsuits.** Families have filed personal-injury suits alleging that popular games, Fortnite among them, were designed to be addictive for children. Every claim above is an allegation unless a court has ruled on it.

### Case details

**FTC refunds:** a **$245 million** FTC administrative order, finalized in March 2023. The refund administrator is Rust Consulting, reachable at 1-833-915-0880. The **$275 million** COPPA penalty came through a separate federal court order filed by the Department of Justice.  
  
**Apple:** *Epic Games, Inc. v. Apple Inc.*, No. 4:20-cv-05640-YGR, U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. Ninth Circuit No. 25-2935, decided December 11, 2025. U.S. Supreme Court No. 25-1311, *Apple Inc. v. Epic Games, Inc.*, on the [Supreme Court docket](https://www.supremecourt.gov/search.aspx?filename=/docket/docketfiles/html/public/25-1311.html).  
  
**Google:** *Epic Games, Inc. v. Google LLC*, No. 3:20-cv-05671-JD, Northern District of California, Judge James Donato, coordinated with *In re Google Play Store Antitrust Litigation*, No. 3:21-md-02981-JD. Ninth Circuit No. 24-6256, decided July 31, 2025.  
  
**Netherlands:** the claim is brought by Stichting Massaschade & Consument (SMC), which says it will go to court if talks with Epic fail.

## Status on September 30, 2026: Nothing New to File

**Fortnite refunds — waiting for round 3.** Claims closed **July 9, 2025**. In June 2025 the FTC sent **969,173 payments totaling more than $126 million**. Its page still says: “We expect to send additional payments in 2026 after we have reviewed and validated all claims.” As of September 30, 2026 it gives no date and still carries a July 2025 date stamp. If you filed after February 14, 2025, the FTC says you do not need to do anything else right now while it reviews claims. Full details: [our Fortnite refund page](/fortnite-ftc-refund) and [our report on the delayed third round](/news/fortnite-ftc-refund-third-round-408-days-after-claims-closed).  
  
**Apple — at the Supreme Court.** On December 11, 2025 the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding but reversed parts of the sanctions, including the outright ban on any Apple commission on purchases made through outside links. On **June 30, 2026** the Supreme Court agreed to hear Apple’s appeal, limited to one question about contempt. Apple filed its brief on September 14; Epic’s is due **November 13, 2026**. No argument date appears on the docket yet. On August 13, 2026, Justice Kagan refused Apple’s request to pause the trial court proceedings.  
  
**Google — verdict stands, deal withdrawn.** The Ninth Circuit affirmed the verdict and injunction on July 31, 2025, and the Supreme Court let the order take effect in October 2025. A settlement announced in November 2025 and revised in March 2026 needed Judge Donato’s approval; according to Gizmodo, Google and Epic withdrew it in July 2026 after the judge voiced skepticism. In August 2026, Aptoide Games became the first rival app store offered inside Google Play in the U.S.  
  
**Player lawsuits.** The Dutch claim is at the demand stage: SMC served Epic with a notice of liability and offered to negotiate. For the U.S. Item Shop timer suit and the addiction suits, we found no settlement and no claim form.

## Which Case Could Involve You

**FTC refund:** it covered players charged in-game currency for items they did not want (January 2017 to September 2022), parents whose child made charges to their card without their knowledge (January 2017 to November 2018), and players whose accounts were locked after disputing charges (January 2017 to September 2022). It only helps you now if you **filed by July 9, 2025**. No new claims are accepted.  
  
**Apple and Google cases:** you are not a party and cannot join. Their outcome changes how app stores handle payment links, fees and rival stores. It does not send money to players. The **$700 million Google Play settlement** is a different case brought by the states, and it pays automatically: see [our Google lawsuit guide](/google-lawsuit).  
  
**Dutch claim:** SMC represents Dutch players who played Fortnite before age 21. It does not cover U.S. players.  
  
**U.S. Item Shop suit and addiction suits:** there is nothing to sign up for. The addiction cases are individual personal-injury suits, not a fund you join; a class action includes you automatically if a class is ever certified or a settlement is reached, and notice would come from a court-appointed administrator.

## What Anyone Has Actually Been Paid

**FTC refunds — the only real money so far.** Round 1 in December 2024 averaged about **$114** per payment; round 2 in June 2025 works out to roughly **$130**. The FTC describes the total sent as “nearly $200 million.” It has not published an amount for round 3, and says each payment depends on factors including how many people filed. Checks must be cashed within 90 days and PayPal payments accepted within 30 days.  
  
**The $275 million COPPA penalty** is a civil penalty, not a refund fund. No player or parent receives any of it.  
  
**Apple and Google cases:** no money for consumers. They are about app store rules.  
  
**Dutch claim:** SMC seeks over **€100 million** in refunds and damages for Dutch players. Nothing has been agreed or awarded.  
  
**U.S. Item Shop suit and addiction suits:** no settlement, no fund, no claim form. Any dollar figure you see attached to them is a guess.

### How cases like this one end

Our copy of the federal courts’ own case database covers 6,924antitrust casesclosed in U.S. federal district courts between 2015and 2026, 37.3% of them filed as class actions:

* •**19.1%** ended in a settlement recorded by the court. Another 14.5% were dismissed voluntarily, which often follows a private settlement — so the real settlement share sits between 19.1% and 33.6%.
* •**11.4%** were decided on a motion before any trial.
* •**1 in 119** reached a trial (0.8%), after a median of 37.1 months.
* •Median time from filing to the end of the case: **11.9 months**.
* •Almost none record a money award in this data (33 of 6,924), and the recorded figures are capped, so we do not publish an average.

These are base rates for this type of case(federal antitrust cases)— not a prediction about this lawsuit, and not legal advice. Source: Federal Judicial Center, Integrated Database (civil), analysed by Settlement Insight. Cases heard in state courts are not included.

## Epic Games Lawsuits Timeline

1. ### August 13, 2020 — Fortnite Pulled From Both App Stores

   Apple and Google remove Fortnite after Epic changes how players can buy V-Bucks. Epic sues both companies.
2. ### December 2022 — $520 Million FTC Settlement

   Epic agrees to a $245 million refund order over dark patterns and a $275 million COPPA penalty. The refund order is finalized in March 2023.
3. ### December 11, 2023 — Jury Rules for Epic Against Google

   The jury finds for Epic on all eleven counts. In October 2024 Judge Donato orders Google to allow rival app stores on Android.
4. ### April 30, 2025 — Apple Held in Contempt

   Judge Gonzalez Rogers finds Apple violated her 2021 injunction, including by charging a 27% commission on linked-out purchases. Fortnite returns to the U.S. App Store on May 20, 2025.
5. ### July 2025 — Refund Claims Close, Google Loses Appeal

   The last day to file a Fortnite refund claim is July 9, 2025. On July 31, 2025 the Ninth Circuit affirms the verdict against Google.
6. ### June 30, 2026 — Supreme Court Takes Apple’s Appeal

   After the Ninth Circuit largely upheld the contempt finding on December 11, 2025, the Supreme Court agrees to hear one contempt question. Epic’s brief is due November 13, 2026; refund round 3 is still pending.

## Three Things to Watch For

A famous brand, young players and a refund that has been “coming in 2026” for over a year is a combination scammers exploit:

“Join the Epic Games class action” ads

The class action in the September 2026 news is Dutch and covers only Dutch players. There is no U.S. claim form for it. A site asking for your Epic login, card number or a fee to “join” is collecting data, not filing anything.

“Your Fortnite round 3 refund is ready” messages

Claims closed July 9, 2025, so any invitation to file one now is fake. Real payments go only to people who already filed, as a check or PayPal payment. The FTC never demands money; the refund administrator’s number is 1-833-915-0880.

Free V-Bucks or an “App Store refund” from the court cases

FTC refunds are paid in real money, not V-Bucks. The Apple and Google cases pay no consumer anything, so a message offering you a share of an Apple or Google ruling is invented.

## Epic Games Lawsuits: Questions People Actually Ask

Short answers to the questions people ask most about this case.

Is there an Epic Games settlement I can file a claim for right now?

No. The FTC’s Fortnite refund stopped taking claims on July 9, 2025, and none of the other cases has a settlement fund or a claim form as of September 30, 2026. For settlements that are open, see [our list of open class action settlements](/open-class-action-settlements).

When is the third Fortnite refund round?

The FTC says it expects to send additional payments in 2026 once all claims are validated. As of September 30, 2026 it has announced no date and no amount. The [FTC refund page](https://www.ftc.gov/enforcement/refunds/fortnite-refunds) is the only authoritative source; our [Fortnite refund page](/fortnite-ftc-refund) tracks it.

What is the Epic Games lawsuit in the news in September 2026?

A Dutch consumer foundation, Stichting Massaschade & Consument, is seeking over €100 million for Dutch players who played Fortnite before age 21. It points to the Dutch regulator’s 2024 fine of €1,125,000 over Item Shop pressure tactics, which a Rotterdam court upheld in January 2026. Epic says the Item Shop has no timer and that parents can require a PIN for purchases. The claim does not include U.S. players.

What is the Supreme Court deciding in Apple v. Epic Games?

Only whether a court may hold a party in civil contempt for violating an injunction’s “spirit” when the order is silent about the conduct. It is not re-deciding whether Apple is a monopoly, and no money for users is at stake. The United States filed a brief supporting neither side on September 21, 2026.

Did Epic Games win its lawsuit against Google?

Yes. The jury ruled for Epic in December 2023, and the Ninth Circuit affirmed on July 31, 2025. The case produced app store changes, not payments to players. The separate $700 million Google Play consumer settlement is explained in [our Google lawsuit guide](/google-lawsuit).

Is there a Fortnite addiction lawsuit?

Families have filed individual lawsuits alleging that video games were designed to addict children, and Epic is named in some, including a Los Angeles Superior Court case filed April 8, 2025. A federal MDL was denied in June 2024 and again on December 10, 2025. We found no settlement. Related cases: [Minecraft](/minecraft-lawsuit) and [Roblox](/roblox-lawsuit).

Does the $275 million COPPA penalty pay parents?

No. It is a civil penalty for alleged children’s-privacy violations. According to the FTC, the settlement also required Epic to turn voice and text chat off by default for children and teens. Only the separate $245 million refund order pays players.

Is there a lawsuit over Fortnite Item Shop timers?

Yes. In March 2025 two parents filed a proposed class action in a San Francisco court, alleging the countdown timers created fake urgency. Epic said the complaint “contains factual errors” and that it would fight the claims. We could not confirm its current status; no settlement has been announced.

# 9-Year-Old Spends $118,000 on YouTube Ads, Dad’s Job Uncertain

![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/mbell.webp)

[Marcus Bell](https://shattered.io/author/mbell/)

Updated Sep 21, 2026 · 14 min read

A nine-year-old boy running a small Minecraft and Roblox channel called Mighty Mike Plays turned a planned $20 YouTube ad promotion into roughly $118,000 in charges over about three weeks, according to a video his father posted on September 15, 2026. The father, who goes by Dave in the coverage, says the money came off a company credit card that had been saved to the family’s shared Google account after an earlier purchase of Robux, Roblox’s in-game currency. [Tom’s Hardware](https://www.tomshardware.com/video-games/devastated-father-says-his-9-year-old-son-spent-usd118-000-on-youtube-ad-campaigns-for-his-minecraft-channel-using-a-company-credit-card-bill-racked-up-in-just-three-weeks-was-supposed-to-be-one-usd20-promotion), The Register, and several other outlets picked up the story within days, and it has since spread across gaming, parenting, and tech-security circles as a case study in what happens when a payment method with no spending cap sits inside an account a child can open.

The story matters to a hardware and consumer-tech audience for a reason that has nothing to do with YouTube fame: it is a live demonstration of how Google’s unified payments profile links purchases across totally unrelated services, and how little friction stands between “buy some Robux” and “launch four-figure ad campaigns” once a card is saved. As of September 21, 2026, the core financial and employment details rest entirely on Dave’s own account. No outlet has published an invoice, an ad-account screenshot, or a statement from his employer.

## What actually happened, according to the father’s video

Dave’s telling, laid out in a video titled “Message from Dad… Mighty Mike Plays is Over,” starts small. He says he wanted to teach his son a lesson about online marketing and set up what he intended to be a single $20 ad campaign promoting one of the boy’s Minecraft videos. Instead, according to Tom’s Hardware’s reporting, the child kept the campaigns running and expanding, spinning up additional pushes under names like “Mighty Mike” and “Epic Roblox” that targeted his own gameplay uploads. Three weeks later, Dave says his company’s finance department called him into a room with his manager and a corporate representative and showed him a spending table totaling $118,000, all billed to the corporate card.

The origin point, per Dave’s account, traces back further than the ad campaign itself. He says he had previously entered his company card into the family’s Google account to buy Robux for his son. Google’s payment system stores card details in what it calls a [payments profile](https://myaccount.google.com/payments-and-subscriptions), a single record tied to the account that can be reused across Google properties, including Google Ads, Google Play, and YouTube. Once that profile existed, the card was available for the child to use again, this time inside the ad platform, without a second approval step or a spending ceiling attached to the account.

## Why the job-loss headline is getting ahead of the facts

Several headlines writing about this story have framed it as a father who lost his job over his son’s spending. That is not confirmed. The Register describes the incident as having cost Dave “$118,000 and possibly his job,” language that signals uncertainty rather than a finalized outcome. Coverage tracked by outlets including CreatorDB and GadgetReview is consistent on this point: nobody has published a statement from Dave’s employer confirming a termination, a suspension, or a formal repayment demand. Dave himself reportedly says he does not yet know whether he will keep his position or be asked to cover the charges personally, and that the matter has been escalated further up his company’s chain.

That distinction is not a technicality. A private individual’s employment status is a serious claim to get wrong, and every outlet that has covered this story so far has been careful to attribute the $118,000 figure, the meeting with finance, and the uncertainty about next steps to Dave’s own account rather than to independently verified company records. Readers searching for updates on whether Dave was fired should know that, as of this writing, no such confirmation exists in the public record.

## How a saved payment profile turns into a five-figure bill

The mechanism behind this story is mundane by design, which is exactly why it is useful to walk through. Google’s account system separates login from payment in one sense but merges them in another: once a card is added to a Google account’s payments profile, it becomes available to any service tied to that same login, provided the account has the right access level. A parent buying Robux through a browser tab, a Play Store purchase, or a one-off Google Ads test campaign all draw from the same stored card. There is no default mechanism that asks “are you sure you want to reuse the card you saved for Roblox to now buy YouTube advertising,” because from the system’s point of view, it is the same authenticated user making a purchase.

Google Ads accounts, unless a manual budget cap is set at the campaign or account level, will continue serving and billing ads up to whatever the card can absorb. A corporate card, unlike many personal consumer cards, often carries a high limit and few automated fraud triggers for a category like online advertising, since ad spend is a routine business expense. That combination, a shared login, a stored high-limit card, and an ad platform with no default daily ceiling, is what allowed a nine-year-old to scale a $20 experiment into six figures without hitting a single blocking prompt.

## This is not the first time a child has run up a parent’s bill

Stories about children racking up charges on a parent’s saved card are a recurring genre, usually involving in-app purchases in mobile games. Regulators including the [FTC’s consumer protection division](https://www.consumer.ftc.gov) have pursued major enforcement actions against Apple, Google, and Amazon over exactly this pattern in the past decade, requiring all three companies to refund millions of dollars to parents whose kids made unauthorized in-app purchases without a secondary password step. What sets the Mighty Mike Plays case apart is scale and category. Most prior cases topped out in the hundreds or low thousands of dollars, tied to loot boxes, gems, or coins inside a single game. This case involves a business advertising platform, a corporate financial instrument, and a bill more than a hundred times larger than the typical in-app purchase horror story.

Google publishes its own [family safety guidance](https://safety.google/families/) covering supervised accounts, but Gagadget’s coverage put it plainly in its reporting on the incident: YouTube’s ad platform had nothing built in that would have stopped a nine-year-old from running the spend up once the card was accessible and no cap was set. That is a fair summary of the gap this case exposes. Purchase-approval systems built for consumer app stores, which now typically require a password, biometric confirmation, or a linked child account with spending limits, have no real equivalent inside a self-serve ad platform designed for adult business users.

## Corporate card policy meets a home Google account

From a workplace-policy angle, this case sits in an uncomfortable spot. Most corporate card agreements require the cardholder to use the card only for approved business expenses and to keep card details secure, which typically means not saving them to shared or personal accounts. Dave’s own account, as reported, acknowledges that he entered the card into a personal Google account himself, first for a small Robux purchase, without appreciating that the same stored credential would remain available for a completely different Google product months or weeks later.

That is the crux of why his employment status is unresolved rather than settled. Companies vary widely in how they handle employee mistakes involving misused corporate cards, and outcomes range from a formal warning and repayment plan to termination, depending on internal policy, the amount involved, and whether the spend was judged negligent versus willfully improper. A $118,000 bill is large enough to trigger serious internal review almost anywhere, but “serious review” and “confirmed job loss” are two different things, and only the first is supported by current reporting.

## Comparing this case with known children’s-purchase incidents

| Incident | Platform | Reported amount | Payment method involved | Resolution |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Mighty Mike Plays ad spend (2026) | Google Ads / YouTube | ~$118,000 | Corporate card saved to Google account | Unconfirmed; father’s job status unresolved |
| FTC v. Apple in-app purchases | iOS App Store | $32.5 million in refunds ordered | Saved card, no re-authentication window | Settled; refunds issued to parents |
| FTC v. Google Play in-app purchases | Google Play | $19 million in refunds ordered | Saved card, default purchase window | Settled; refunds issued to parents |
| FTC v. Amazon in-app purchases | Amazon Appstore | $70 million in refunds ordered | Saved card, no password requirement | Settled; refunds issued to parents |

The pattern across every row is the same: a payment method stays authenticated at the account level rather than the transaction level, and a child inside that account inherits the ability to spend without a dedicated checkpoint. The dollar figures in the FTC cases represent aggregate refunds across large user populations rather than single-family incidents, which is what makes the Mighty Mike Plays number so unusual. It is one household, one card, and one three-week window.

## The GoFundMe and crypto question that isn’t happening

Part of why this story has spread so widely is a detail that is notable precisely because it did not happen: Dave has reportedly declined to set up a GoFundMe campaign or accept cryptocurrency donations to help cover the bill, telling viewers in his video that he intends to handle the situation himself. Coverage across the outlets tracking this story, including American Bazaar and Yahoo, does not mention any crowdfunding page, wallet address, or organized repayment drive tied to Dave or his son’s channel. That single choice, refusing outside money for what could be a six-figure personal liability, has become as much a talking point in the response to the story as the original spending figure.

## What a $118,000 ad bill says about self-serve advertising platforms

Google Ads, like Meta’s ad platform and most other self-serve advertising systems, was built for speed. Anyone with a verified payment method can launch a campaign in minutes, set a daily budget, and start driving traffic without human review. That design choice, low friction for advertisers, is a deliberate business decision that has made these platforms enormously profitable and easy to use for small businesses and creators. It also means the guardrails that exist, primarily an optional daily budget cap that the account owner must set manually, are opt-in rather than default.

Nothing in current Google Ads account setup forces a new advertiser to set a hard budget ceiling before a campaign goes live. An account can, in principle, keep spending as long as the linked payment method continues to authorize charges. For a professional marketer managing a five-figure monthly budget, that flexibility is a feature. For a family account where a child has access to the login, it is the exact gap this incident fell through.

## Practical steps to prevent a repeat of this scenario

Security and parenting-focused coverage of this story has converged on a short list of fixes that apply to any household or small business where a high-limit card might end up saved to a shared account. None of these require special software, only a few minutes inside account settings.

* Remove any corporate or high-limit personal card from a Google payments profile that a child or shared device can access, and use a dedicated low-limit prepaid card for kids’ purchases instead.
* Set a hard daily budget cap on any Google Ads account tied to the household, even if no active campaigns are expected.
* Enable [Google’s Family Link](https://support.google.com/families/answer/7101025) or a similar supervised-account structure for a child’s YouTube and Google activity, which restricts purchase and ad-platform access by default.
* Turn on [purchase-approval requests inside Google Play and YouTube settings](https://support.google.com/googleplay/answer/1626831) so any spend triggers a notification to a parent device before it completes.
* Periodically audit the payments profile tied to any shared or work-linked Google account to see which cards are stored and which services can draw from them.
* Treat “enter the card once for a small purchase” as equivalent to “leave the card permanently available,” since that is functionally what a stored payments profile does.

## Employer policy gaps this case exposes

Most corporate card programs rely on expense reporting and periodic statement review to catch misuse, which means a determined or unsupervised spend can run for weeks before anyone in finance notices, exactly the three-week window Dave describes. Companies that want to close this gap have a few concrete options: transaction-level spend alerts that flag any charge to an unfamiliar merchant category like online advertising, hard category blocks that prevent corporate cards from being used on ad platforms at all without prior approval, and mandatory reauthentication whenever a corporate card is added to a personal or shared account. None of these are exotic controls. Most corporate card providers, including major business card issuers, already offer merchant-category restrictions as a configurable option that many companies simply never turn on.

## Market and industry reaction

The story has moved quickly through gaming, parenting, and tech-security media since the September 15 video, picked up by outlets spanning the US, Europe, and Asia, including Tom’s Hardware, The Register, Moneycontrol, Gagadget, Gigazine, unwire.hk, and iXBT Games. That spread reflects how easily the core detail, a child accidentally spending six figures through a stored payment method, travels across language and market boundaries, since the underlying risk (shared logins, saved cards, low-friction ad platforms) is identical everywhere Google Ads operates. Neither Google nor Dave’s employer has issued a public statement responding to the coverage as of September 21, 2026.

## Where the story is likely to go next

A handful of outcomes look plausible based on how similar stories have played out before, though none of the following are confirmed and all should be read as informed predictions rather than reporting.

1. Google faces renewed pressure to add a default spending cap or a mandatory confirmation step to new Google Ads accounts, similar to the changes it made to Play Store purchase approvals after the FTC settlement.
2. Dave’s employer, facing public attention, is more likely to resolve the situation with a repayment plan or written warning than a public termination announcement, since companies generally prefer to keep internal HR matters out of the press once a story has gone viral.
3. Other examples of children racking up large ad-platform charges surface in the coming months, since this case has made the specific vulnerability (saved cards feeding self-serve ad accounts) widely known.
4. Consumer and business card issuers see increased interest in merchant-category locks for advertising platforms as a standard corporate card feature rather than an opt-in extra.
5. The Mighty Mike Plays channel does not return in its prior form, based on the video’s own title indicating the project is ending, though the family could resume content under a different structure with stricter account controls.

## What families and finance teams should watch for

The details still missing from this story are exactly the ones worth tracking. Whether Dave keeps his job, whether the company or Google absorbs any of the $118,000, and whether Google changes its default Ads account setup in response are all open questions. Until an employer statement, a Google response, or additional documentation surfaces, every figure in this story should be treated as Dave’s own account, credible given the consistency across outlets, but not independently verified by financial records.

## Key facts at a glance

| Detail | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Reported ad spend | ~$118,000 over about three weeks |
| Source of the figure | Father’s own video account (September 15, 2026) |
| Platform charged | Google Ads, promoting YouTube videos |
| Card used | Father’s company credit card, saved to family Google account |
| How the card was saved | Earlier Robux (Roblox currency) purchase, per the father |
| Father’s job status | Unconfirmed; described as uncertain by multiple outlets |
| Repayment obligation | Unconfirmed; no employer statement published |
| GoFundMe or crypto donations | None reported; father says he declined to set one up |
| Employer or Google statement | None published as of September 21, 2026 |

## Frequently asked questions

### Did the father in the Mighty Mike Plays story actually lose his job?

That is not confirmed. Coverage describes his employment status as uncertain, based on his own statement that the matter has been escalated within his company and that he does not yet know the outcome. No employer has publicly confirmed a termination.

### How did a nine-year-old get access to a company credit card?

According to the father, he entered the card into the family’s shared Google account to buy Robux for his son. That saved the card in Google’s payments profile, making it available for later purchases on other Google services, including Google Ads, without a separate approval step.

### Is the $118,000 figure independently verified?

No. Every outlet covering the story attributes the figure to the father’s own video and account of a meeting with his company’s finance department. No invoice, ad account screenshot, or company statement has been published to independently confirm the total.

### Is this the same as kids buying loot boxes or in-app currency?

The underlying mechanism, a saved payment method with no spending checkpoint, is similar to cases the FTC pursued against Apple, Google Play, and Amazon over unauthorized in-app purchases by children. The scale is different: this case involves a self-serve ad platform and a corporate card rather than a consumer app store purchase.

### Can Google Ads accounts be set up with a spending limit?

Yes, account owners can set daily budget caps on individual campaigns, but there is no mandatory default limit that applies automatically when an account is created, which is part of what allowed the spend in this case to continue unchecked.

### Has Google responded to the story?

No public statement from Google had been reported as of September 21, 2026.

### Is the Mighty Mike Plays channel still active?

The video announcing the incident was titled “Message from Dad… Mighty Mike Plays is Over,” suggesting the channel is ending in its current form, though no outlet has reported a permanent deletion.

### What should parents do to avoid a similar situation?

Remove high-limit or corporate cards from shared Google payments profiles, use a dedicated low-limit card for children’s purchases, enable Family Link or similar supervised-account controls, and set hard budget caps on any advertising account linked to the household.

# Adobe FTC Lawsuit: 2026 Settlement Explained

•[News](/c/news)•[Gabriel E. Hall](/author/gabriel-e-hall)

![Adobe FTC Lawsuit: 2026 Settlement Explained](/pic/w3840q75/uploads/wp/news/adobe-targeted-by-ftc-due-to-decetive-sub-cancellation-practices-copy_en.jpg.webp)

Adobe agreed to a $150 million settlement in March 2026 over its hidden cancellation fee. What the FTC case alleged, what changed and what to check.

At a glance

## Adobe and the FTC in 2026: the short answer

The FTC case against Adobe ended in a settlement. On March 13, 2026 the Justice Department announced that Adobe agreed to pay $75 million in civil penalties and offer customers $75 million in free services, a total of $150 million, to resolve claims that it hid an early termination fee and made cancelling hard.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) Adobe said it disagrees with the government's claims and denies any wrongdoing.[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026)

The deal comes as a proposed stipulated order that still needs a court to enter it, according to the Justice Department.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) We found no later page that says whether the court has entered it, so check the case docket if you need the final status. The case also named two Adobe executives, Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, and the same order is meant to resolve the claims against them.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)

Adobe and the FTC case at a glance| Question | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| What was alleged | Hiding the early termination fee (ETF) and making cancellation hard, a violation of ROSCA[[1]](#cite-ftc-1)[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| The ETF | 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if you cancel in the first year of an annual plan paid monthly[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| Outcome | Proposed settlement announced March 13, 2026[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |
| Money | $75 million civil penalty plus $75 million in free services[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |
| Adobe's position | Disagrees with the claims and denies wrongdoing[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) |
| Court | U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |

## Timeline: from Figma to a $150 million settlement

![Timeline of the Adobe FTC case from the September 2022 Figma deal and the 2023 breakup fee to the 2024 complaint and the March 2026 settlement of 150 million dollars](/pic/w1080q75/uploads/news/adobe-ftc-ftc-lawsuit-timeline-2026.png.webp "Timeline of the Adobe subscription case, 2022 to 2026")

Timeline of the Adobe subscription case, 2022 to 2026. Sources: The Verge, Variety, FTC, Justice Department, Reuters.

Dated events in the Adobe case| Date | Event |
| --- | --- |
| September 15, 2022 | The Verge reports Adobe will buy Figma in a deal worth $20 billion[[5]](#cite-the-verge-5) |
| Late 2023 | Adobe drops the Figma bid citing regulatory opposition and pays a $1 billion breakup fee[[6]](#cite-variety-6) |
| June 2024 | The FTC takes action against Adobe and two executives over the hidden ETF and cancellation process[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) |
| June 2024 | Adobe publishes a statement responding to the complaint[[4]](#cite-adobe-4) |
| March 13, 2026 | The Justice Department announces the $150 million settlement and injunction[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) |

## What changed since 2024

In 2024 this was an allegation. The 2024 complaint said Adobe showed the monthly price clearly but buried the ETF in fine print and behind small icons.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2) Now there is a negotiated outcome, with money and rules attached.

The Justice Department says the order requires Adobe to give subscribers easy ways to cancel. Adobe must also clearly disclose any ETF and how it is calculated before enrolling customers. It must remind customers before a free trial longer than seven days turns into a paid plan with an ETF.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement)

Reuters reports that Adobe said it was pleased to resolve the matter while denying wrongdoing.[[8]](#reuters-adobe-settlement-2026) Nothing in the sources we read says Adobe admitted fault. Our original report below describes the complaint as filed in 2024 and is kept unchanged.

## Risks around subscription traps (our analysis)

Our analysis is that the Adobe case is a pattern, and the same traps appear in many apps. Watch for these.

* **Plans that look monthly but are annual.** The headline price says monthly while the contract runs for a year, as the FTC described.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)
* **Cancellation fees in small print.** Look for an early termination fee line before you press buy and note how it is calculated.
* **Free trials that turn paid.** The settlement terms include a reminder before a long trial converts to a paid plan with an ETF.[[7]](#doj-adobe-rosca-settlement) Set your own calendar reminder anyway.
* **Fake cancellation or refund pages.** Scammers imitate subscription support and ask for card details. Always cancel from the official account page and read our [phishing report guide](/how-to/report-phishing).

## Steps if you have an Adobe or similar subscription

![Six steps for software subscribers: read the plan terms, check the fee, set a trial reminder, cancel from the account page, keep proof, watch card statements](/pic/w1080q75/uploads/news/adobe-ftc-ftc-lawsuit-steps-2026.png.webp "Six steps to avoid subscription traps")

Six steps to avoid subscription traps. 2-Spyware, 2026.

**1. Read the plan type.** Check whether a monthly price hides a year-long commitment. Adobe's own page explains its subscription terms and refund policy.[[3]](#cite-adobe-3)

**2. Find the fee.** Look for any early termination fee. In the FTC complaint, it was 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments when cancelling in year one.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)

**3. Set a trial reminder.** Put the end date of any free trial in your calendar. Do not rely on the company to remind you.

**4. Cancel in your account.** Use the company's own account page. Do not follow links from emails or ads that claim to cancel for you.

**5. Keep proof.** Save the cancellation confirmation email and take screenshots of each page.

**6. Watch your statements.** If billing continues after you cancelled, contact the company in writing and then your card issuer. You can also check if your email was exposed with our [leak check](/check).

## What is still unknown

* Whether the court has entered the proposed order. We found no confirmation after March 13, 2026.
* How customers will receive the $75 million in free services. The pages we read do not describe the process.
* Whether other subscription companies face similar cases. We found nothing we could confirm.

## Our original 2024 report

The text below is our report as first published in 2024. We keep it unchanged for the record; the sections above bring it up to date.

Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has filed a complaint[[1]](#cite-ftc-1) against Adobe and two of its executives, Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.

The complaint accuses Adobe of deceptive practices related to its subscription plans, specifically failing to disclose early termination fees (ETFs) and making the cancellation process unnecessarily complicated.[[2]](#cite-ftc-2)

FTC alleges that these practices violate the Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act (ROSCA), which requires clear disclosure of all terms and a straightforward cancellation mechanism.

## Cancellation fees are hidden behind fine print

Adobe transitioned to a subscription model in 2012, requiring users to pay regularly for access to its software, including popular products like Photoshop and Acrobat.

FTC's complaint details how Adobe steers consumers towards its "annual paid monthly" subscription plan without adequately informing them about the ETF, which can be as much as 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if canceled within the first year.[[3]](#cite-adobe-3)

This fee is often hidden in fine print or behind small icons on Adobe's website. Consumers reported to FTC and the Better Business Bureau that they were unaware of the ETF or the requirement to keep the subscription for a year. Adobe's failure to disclose these terms clearly is central to FTC's allegations.

## Deceptive practices when users decide to cancel their subscriptions

The complaint also describes Adobe's cancellation process as intentionally complex, designed to deter consumers from canceling their subscriptions.

When attempting to cancel, consumers must navigate through multiple pages on Adobe's website, starting with locating the account management page, clicking on "Manage Plan," and then selecting "Cancel Your Plan."

Even after reaching this point, users are often forced to re-enter their password and complete a mandatory feedback page that prominently displays the ETF, effectively discouraging cancellation.

Furthermore, FTC alleges that Adobe's customer service adds to the difficulties by frequently dropping calls, disconnecting chats, and transferring customers between representatives, forcing them to re-explain their cancellation request each time. Consumers also reported continued billing despite believing they had canceled their subscriptions, further exacerbating their frustration.

## FTC seeks appropriate actions from Adobe

FTC's complaint seeks several forms of relief to address these issues. These include a permanent injunction to stop ongoing violations, monetary civil penalties for ROSCA violations, restitution for affected consumers, and the cancellation or modification of existing contracts entered into under deceptive terms.

The complaint also targets Adobe executives Sawhney, Senior Vice President of Digital Go To Market & Sales, and Wadhwani, President of Digital Media Business, accusing them of being aware of and continuing the unlawful practices.

Commission voted 3-0 to refer the civil penalty complaint to the Department of Justice (DOJ) for filing. The DOJ then filed the complaint, which will be decided by the court.

## Adobe denies the allegations

In response to FTC's action, Adobe has disputed the allegations. Dana Rao, Adobe's General Counsel and Chief Trust Officer, stated:[[4]](#cite-adobe-4)

> We are transparent with the terms and conditions of our subscription agreements and have a simple cancellation process. We will refute FTC's claims in court.

Adobe maintains that its subscription services are convenient, flexible, and cost-effective, allowing users to choose the plan that best fits their needs, timeline, and budget.

The lawsuit against Adobe highlights the broader regulatory scrutiny of subscription practices and consumer protection. The federal government began investigating Adobe's cancellation practices late last year, and this case is part of a larger effort to ensure companies do not use deceptive tactics to trap consumers in long-term subscriptions.

Adobe's recent attempt to acquire the product design platform Figma for $20 billion[[5]](#cite-the-verge-5) faced antitrust scrutiny, reflecting continued regulatory challenges for the company.[[6]](#cite-variety-6)

FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection Director Samuel Levine said that deceptive cancellation fees should stop being practiced, saying:

> Americans are tired of companies hiding the ball during subscription signup and then putting up roadblocks when they try to cancel. FTC will continue working to protect Americans from these illegal business practices.

Was Adobe sued by the FTC?

Yes. The FTC took action against Adobe and two executives in June 2024, alleging a hidden early termination fee and a hard cancellation process.{2} The case later ended in a proposed settlement that the Justice Department announced on March 13, 2026.{7}

How much is the Adobe settlement?

It is $150 million in total. The Justice Department says the proposed order requires $75 million in civil penalties and $75 million in free services for customers.{7} Adobe says it denies any wrongdoing.{8}

What is the Adobe hidden cancellation fee?

It is the early termination fee on the annual paid monthly plan. The FTC said it equals 50 percent of the remaining monthly payments if you cancel during the first year, and that Adobe buried it in fine print.{2}

What happened to the Adobe executives in the case?

The case named Maninder Sawhney and David Wadhwani, and the Justice Department says the proposed stipulated order is meant to resolve the case against Adobe and both employees.{7} We found no further detail on them.

# Sextortion Email Scams

If you got an email claiming a hacker recorded you through your webcam and will send the video to everyone you know unless you pay in Bitcoin, it’s almost certainly a mass scam. Don’t pay, don’t reply, and change the password the email mentions.

By **the CITA Editorial Team**Updated October 2, 20267 min read

These emails are built to frighten you into paying before you stop to think. Here is how to recognize one, why it can mention your real password or even show your house, and the rare signs that a threat is real.

Fast Facts About Sextortion Email Scams

* The FBI says these emails threaten to release explicit videos to your contacts unless you pay, often in Bitcoin, and may quote one of your passwords to seem believable.[[1]](#sources)
* The FTC calls the hacking claims “all talk.” The password usually comes from an old data breach.[[2]](#sources)
* Newer versions add your name, address and a photo of your house. Police say the scammer still doesn’t have access to your device.[[3]](#sources)
* The FBI received more than 75,000 sextortion reports in 2025. People 60 and older reported the largest losses, nearly $15 million.[[4]](#sources)
* Report these emails to the FBI at ic3.gov and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)

## What Is a Sextortion Email?

A sextortion email is a blackmail message sent to huge numbers of people at once. It claims the sender has sexual images or video of you, often recorded while you watched adult websites, and threatens to send it to your friends, family or coworkers unless you pay.[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)

It’s different from the sextortion that targets teens, where a real person builds a relationship, gets an image and then demands money or more images. That kind involves a real conversation and real images, and it calls for different steps. If that’s what is happening to your child, go to the [sextortion guide](/online-safety/sextortion/) now.

## What These Emails Usually Say

The wording changes, but most versions include several of these:

* A password of yours, real but usually old, in the subject line or the first sentence[[1]](#sources)
* A claim that malware or remote access let them record you through your camera[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)
* A claim that they watched you visit adult websites[[2]](#sources)
* A demand for payment in Bitcoin, with a wallet address or QR code[[1]](#sources)[[3]](#sources)
* A deadline, often 24 to 48 hours[[3]](#sources)
* Your name, home address, phone number or a photo of your house[[3]](#sources)
* A sender address that looks like your own email account

## How to Tell If a Sextortion Email Is Real

Almost all of these emails are bluffs. These signs point to a scam:

* **There’s no actual image.** The email describes a video but never shows you a frame of it, because there isn’t one.[[2]](#sources)
* **The password is old.** If you recognize a password you stopped using years ago, it most likely came from a data breach, not your computer.[[2]](#sources)
* **The details are generic.** Nothing in it is specific to you beyond what’s in a breach or public records: no real contact names, no description of you.
* **The same text appears online.** Search a sentence from the email in quotes. These messages are sent in bulk, so the same wording usually turns up in many other people’s reports.
* **It demands cryptocurrency on a tight deadline.** Urgency is meant to stop you from checking.[[1]](#sources)[[3]](#sources)

### When a Threat Might Be Real

Take a threat seriously if you actually shared intimate images with someone, or if there are signs someone has broken into your accounts. In August 2026 the FBI warned that criminals are getting into people’s social media and cloud accounts to steal real explicit images and post them, sometimes with the victim’s name and other personal details.[[5]](#sources) Watch for:

* Texts claiming your account will be locked unless you reply with a verification code[[5]](#sources)
* Emails from look-alike “support” addresses about new logins[[5]](#sources)
* Login alerts or password resets you didn’t request

If any of that applies, secure your accounts right away, report to the FBI at [ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/), and follow the steps in the section below on real images.[[5]](#sources)

## Why the Email Has Your Password

When a website is breached, lists of email addresses and passwords end up for sale. Scammers buy those lists, then paste the password into a blackmail email to make the hacking claim seem believable. The FTC’s advice: the hacking story is “all talk,” but if the password is one you still use, change it on that account and anywhere else you reused it.[[2]](#sources)

To see which of your accounts have shown up in breaches, use the password checkup built into Google’s and Apple’s password managers, or a breach-search service such as Have I Been Pwned.

## Why It Looks Like It Came From Your Own Address

The “from” line on an email is easy to fake. The FBI calls this spoofing: disguising an email address or sender name so a message seems to come from someone it doesn’t.[[6]](#sources) An email that appears to come from your own address doesn’t mean anyone is inside your account. Changing your password and turning on two-step verification is still a good idea.[[8]](#sources)

## Why Some Emails Include a Photo of Your House

A newer version adds your name, your address and a picture of your home, which feels like proof that someone has been watching you. New York State Police warned about this version in 2024. They said scammers buy people’s personal information illegally online, and that despite the threats, “the scammer does not have access to the victim’s device or personal information.”[[3]](#sources) Street-level photos of most homes are publicly viewable on online map services, so a picture of your house is easy to find.

## What to Do If You Get a Sextortion Email

1. **Don’t pay.** There’s no video for them to delete, and people who pay scammers end up on lists that other scammers buy.[[2]](#sources)[[7]](#sources)
2. **Don’t reply or click anything.** Don’t open attachments or links, and don’t share personal or financial details.[[1]](#sources)[[3]](#sources)
3. **Change the password it shows**, and any other account where you used it.[[2]](#sources)
4. **Turn on two-step verification** for your email, social media and cloud accounts.[[5]](#sources)[[8]](#sources)
5. **Report it** to the FBI at [ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/) and to the FTC at [ReportFraud.ftc.gov](https://reportfraud.ftc.gov/).[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)
6. **Block the sender and delete the email** once you’ve reported it.[[3]](#sources)

### If You Already Paid

Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov with the date, the amount and the wallet address you paid. Then be ready for a second scam. The FTC warns that people who have lost money are often targeted by “recovery” schemes promising to get the money back for an upfront fee. Anyone who asks you to pay to recover money you lost is running a scam.[[7]](#sources)

## If Someone Really Has Your Images

If the threat involves real images, because you shared them with someone or an account was broken into, the same rules apply: don’t pay, stop responding, and save the messages. Then:

* Report to the FBI at [ic3.gov](https://www.ic3.gov/).[[5]](#sources)
* Use [StopNCII.org](https://stopncii.org/) to help block intimate images of adults from being posted on participating platforms.[[10]](#sources)
* If an image is posted, ask the platform to remove it. Under the [Take It Down Act](/online-safety/take-it-down-act/), covered platforms must take it down within 48 hours of a valid request.[[10]](#sources)
* If the images show someone under 18, follow the [sextortion guide](/online-safety/sextortion/) and report to the NCMEC CyberTipline.[[9]](#sources)

If you feel overwhelmed or unsafe, call or text 988, any time.[[11]](#sources)

## Help an Older Parent Spot These Emails

Older adults lose the most to sextortion. In 2025, people 60 and older reported nearly $15 million in sextortion losses to the FBI, more than any other age group.[[4]](#sources) Shame keeps many people from asking anyone before they pay. A short conversation ahead of time helps:

* Show them what one of these emails looks like, so the first one they see isn’t a shock.
* Tell them the rule plainly: anyone demanding Bitcoin to keep a video secret is a scammer, and the video doesn’t exist.
* Make it easy to ask. “Forward me anything that scares you, no questions asked” removes the embarrassment.
* Help them set up two-step verification and change any reused passwords.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I be worried about a sextortion email?

Almost never. Mass sextortion emails are bluffs sent to huge lists of addresses, and the hacking and webcam claims are false. The one real risk is a password from an old breach, so change it.[[2]](#sources)[[3]](#sources)

### Should I ignore a sextortion email?

Don’t reply or pay, but don’t just ignore it either. Change the password it mentions, report it to ic3.gov and ReportFraud.ftc.gov, then block the sender and delete it.[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)[[3]](#sources)

### Can a hacker really record me through my webcam?

Not in these scams. The FTC calls those claims “all talk.”[[2]](#sources) Unique passwords and two-step verification protect you against real account break-ins, which are a separate threat.[[5]](#sources)

### Why do I keep getting sextortion emails?

Your email address is probably on lists sold after data breaches, and scammers send the same message to everyone on those lists again and again.[[2]](#sources)[[3]](#sources) Marking them as spam helps your email provider filter future ones.

### What if I already paid?

Report it to the FBI at ic3.gov with the date, amount and wallet address. Don’t pay anyone who offers to recover the money for a fee. The FTC says that’s a common follow-up scam.[[7]](#sources)

### Where do I report a sextortion email?

Report to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at ic3.gov and to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.[[1]](#sources)[[2]](#sources)

## Related Guides

## Contents

# *Epic Games v. Apple*

| Epic Games v. Apple | |

| Argued | May 3–24, 2021 |
| Decided | September 10, 2021 |
| Holding | |
